topics.name: Verb Tenses
topics.summary: Past, present and future, and keeping them consistent.

objectives.text: Identify the tense of a verb.
Change a sentence from one tense to another.
Keep tense consistent within a piece of writing.

keyTerms.definition: The form of a verb that shows when something happens.
A verb whose past form does not simply add -ed, such as go → went.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body: The same action can happen yesterday, now, or tomorrow, and the verb changes to show which. This lesson is about making that choice deliberately instead of by accident.

sections.heading: The three tenses
sections.body:
PRESENT — happening now, or happening regularly.
    I walk to school.
    She walks to school.

PAST — already happened.
    I walked to school.

FUTURE — has not happened yet.
    I will walk to school.

Most verbs form the past by adding -ed, and the future by putting "will" in front. Only the verb changes — the rest of the sentence can stay the same.

sections.heading: Irregular verbs
sections.body:
Some common verbs do not follow the -ed rule, and these are the ones people get wrong:

    go   → went    (not "goed")
    eat  → ate     (not "eated")
    see  → saw
    take → took
    come → came
    write → wrote

There is no rule to work these out — they have to be learned. They are also the most common verbs in the language, which is why they are worth learning properly.

sections.heading: Keep the tense consistent
sections.body:
This is the mistake that costs marks most often. Once you choose a tense, stay in it unless the time genuinely changes.

    Wrong: Yesterday I went to the market and buy rice.
           "went" is past, "buy" is present. They disagree.

    Right:  Yesterday I went to the market and bought rice.

When you finish a piece of writing, read it once looking ONLY at the verbs. Ignore everything else. Tense mistakes hide easily inside a sentence that otherwise sounds fine.
sections.example:
Changing one sentence through all three tenses.

    Present: The farmer plants cassava.
    Past:    The farmer planted cassava.
    Future:  The farmer will plant cassava.

Now one with an irregular verb:

    Present: She writes a letter.
    Past:    She wrote a letter.      (not "writed")
    Future:  She will write a letter.

Notice that after "will", the verb goes back to its plain form — "will write", never "will wrote".

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
Change each into the past tense:
1. We eat rice every evening.
2. He goes to the farm.
3. They see the river.

Then fix this: "Last week my sister travel to town and buys new shoes."

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• Present = now, past = already happened, future = not yet.
• Most verbs add -ed for past and "will" for future.
• Irregular verbs (go/went, eat/ate) must be learned.
• After "will", use the plain verb form.
• Stay in one tense; check by reading only the verbs.

questions.question: What is the past tense of "go"?
questions.explanation: "Went" — "go" is an irregular verb, so it does not add -ed. "Gone" is used with a helper verb ("has gone"), not on its own for simple past. Irregular verbs have to be learned; there is no rule to work them out.

questions.question: What is wrong with: "Yesterday I went to the market and buy rice"?
options: The tenses do not match — "buy" should be "bought"
questions.explanation: "Went" is past but "buy" is present, so the tenses disagree. It should be "went... and bought". Read a finished piece looking ONLY at the verbs — tense mistakes hide easily inside sentences that otherwise sound fine.
